_doc: Hours a household's own work takes a year, by task (Complaint 645). A household meets these with its own hours or hires them (the domestic_servant trade; the household_work need in needs.json). Cooking needs a hearth and fuel: a household without one buys cooked food instead (sim/economy/households_work.py). Hours are per person of the household, worked from a per-day figure.
cooking_fuel_basis: Fuelwood burnt in household cookstoves in an isolated rural West African village fell 'from 20.6 MJ cap-1 day-1 to 10.5 MJ cap-1 day-1' as household size rose from five to 20 (Nathan G. Johnson and Kenneth M. Bryden, 'Factors affecting fuelwood consumption in household cookstoves in an isolated rural West African village', Energy 46(1), 2012, pp. 310-321; abstract opened; stove type and sample size not given there). The five-person figure is taken, as the household size of climate_needs.PERSONS_PER_HOUSEHOLD. Megajoules of fuel heat, the unit of the warmth need; added to a hearth's warmth floor. One village, open stoves: confidence C.
supervision_basis: Hours of a household's own it spends directing and checking each hour a servant works for it. No source found: a labelled estimate, confidence D. The servant's keep is already in the price an hour of service sells at (the servant's wage and the cost of what makes the service).
supervision_retire: Complaints/645 follow-up: a time-use or servant-management source for the hours a household spends directing servants, then derive it from the servant's hours and the household's staff

water_and_fuel.basis: Rural Burkina Faso, average minutes a day for women (Box 1, 'Rural activities, comparison of time allocation by sex, Burkina Faso', source line 'Carr and Sandhu, 1988', in A Gordon, A Swetman and K Albright, 'Women in post-harvest operations: reducing the drudgery', Issues Paper 6, June 2002, p. 2; opened; a secondary reproduction, survey year and sample not given there): water supply 38 minutes and fuel supply 6 minutes, 44 minutes a day. A fixed load: no market good stands in for fetching. The earlier figure took only the carrying range of Blackden and Wodon (eds), Gender, Time Use, and Poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa, World Bank Working Paper 73, 2006, overview p. 9: 'These figures equate to a time input for an average adult female ranging from just under 1 hour to 2 hours 20 minutes every day'. Adult women as a quarter of a household's people: no source found, confidence D.

grinding.basis: Rural Burkina Faso, average minutes a day for women (Box 1, 'Rural activities, comparison of time allocation by sex, Burkina Faso', source line 'Carr and Sandhu, 1988', in A Gordon, A Swetman and K Albright, 'Women in post-harvest operations: reducing the drudgery', Issues Paper 6, June 2002, p. 2; opened; a secondary reproduction, survey year and sample not given there): grinding and pounding grain 108 minutes a day. The two lines sum to 152 minutes a day (the earlier single task rounded that to 2.5 hours). Grinding is a way of making flour, so a household bears it only on the grain it grinds itself: the hours are scaled by the share of its food it grinds by hand, and a household that can buy flour for less than its hours are worth buys it (sim/economy/household_grinding.py). The table gives no kilograms ground, so the full load is taken as the grinding of a diet wholly of grain at the food floor. Adult women as a quarter of a household's people: no source found, confidence D.
grinding.retire: Complaints/645 follow-up: kilograms of grain ground per hour by hand from a grain-processing study, replacing the assumption that the surveyed load ground a diet wholly of grain

cooking.basis: Ghana 2009 national time-use diary, women aged 15-59, mean 18.1 hours a week in cooking (food preparation, clean up, fetching wood and water), 2.6 hours a day; Sierra Leone 2003 labour force survey, 8.7 hours a week (Taryn Dinkelman and L. Rachel Ngai, 'Time Use and Gender in Africa in Times of Structural Transformation', Journal of Economic Perspectives 36(1), 2022, pp. 57-80; Online Data Appendix, Table A.1, 'Weekly Hours in Home Production among All Women'; appendix opened, the article itself not). Ghana is taken: a diary survey that counts secondary activities. It is a national sample with some piped water and mills, so not a pure subsistence household, and its cooking category includes some wood and water fetching, which the water_fuel_and_grinding task also counts. Adult women as a quarter of a household's people: no source found, confidence D.
cooking.retire: Complaints/645 follow-up: a share of adult women per household from a demographic source, and a time-use survey of a society without piped water or mills

cleaning_and_childcare.basis: Ghana 2009 national time-use diary, women aged 15-59, mean weekly hours: cleaning 2.4, laundry 2.4, care of children and adults 7.8, together 12.6 hours a week, 1.8 hours a day; Sierra Leone 2003 sums to 19.2 (Dinkelman and Ngai, JEP 36(1), 2022, Online Data Appendix, Table A.1; appendix opened). Household management (shopping, travel) is left out. Ghana is taken, with the caveats of the cooking task. Adult women as a quarter of a household's people: no source found, confidence D.
cleaning_and_childcare.retire: Complaints/645 follow-up: a share of adult women per household from a demographic source, and a time-use survey of a society without piped water or mills
